source: Goodman, Mansinghka, Roy, Bonawitz, Tenenbaum (2008) Church: a language for generative models
finding: Church is a Lisp-like language based on lambda calculus. Evaluation is sampling. A query is conditional sampling. Any generative process can be written as a program.
numbers: Paper at UAI 2008, pp. 220-229. Five authors from MIT BCS/CSAIL. Core design: stochastic primitives, lex-query, and stochastic memoization (mem).
quote: view evaluation as sampling and query as conditional sampling
limits: Early MIT-Church interpreter. The paper gives worked examples and sketches, not human-data tests.
agent_relevance: Models of thought as code plus conditioning is the template for scaffold steps that sample a world model, then condition on evidence.

source: Goodman, Mansinghka, Roy, Bonawitz, Tenenbaum (2008) Church: a language for generative models
finding: The stochastic memoizer mem makes random draws persistent per argument. So (= (rain 'day2) (rain 'day2)) is always True. This lets a program name latent causes that stay fixed across a query.
numbers: Sprinkler/rain/grass-wet example. Draw weights from a Beta(1,1) hyper-prior with mem and the program learns the weights from other days' observations.
limits: Memoization is semantically subtle: the paper proves admissibility (weights converge and are bounded by 1) only under conditions.
agent_relevance: Persistent named latents let an agent keep one consistent hypothesis across many sub-questions.

source: Goodman, Mansinghka, Roy, Bonawitz, Tenenbaum (2008) Church: a language for generative models
finding: DPmem (Dirichlet-process memoizer) is written inside Church by stick-breaking. With concentration a=0 it reduces to mem. With a=infinity it reduces to the identity. It gives infinite mixture models, infinite relational models, HDP-PCFG and HDP-HMM in a few lines.
numbers: Models shown: infinite Gaussian mixture, IRM, HDP-PCFG, HDP-HMM (100-sided die observations), adapted PCFG via DPmem of unfold.
limits: Only forward-sampling code is shown for the mixture models. No timing or fit numbers.
agent_relevance: Open-ended hypothesis classes (new categories) can be expressed without fixing their number in advance.

source: Goodman, Mansinghka, Roy, Bonawitz, Tenenbaum (2008) Church: a language for generative models
finding: Planning is posed as inference. A 'red-light' game is solved by conditioning on reward and reading off the first action, following Toussaint et al.'s planning-as-inference translation.
numbers: Reward prediction is flip(mean reward). Discount handled by a flip(gamma) termination test.
limits: Authors note the resulting choices are fairly random in the toy game and plain rejection is inefficient.
agent_relevance: Plan selection as conditioning on success is a candidate pattern: treat the goal as evidence.

source: Goodman, Mansinghka, Roy, Bonawitz, Tenenbaum (2008) Church: a language for generative models
finding: Inference: a collapsed rejection sampler follows directly from the semantics. A Metropolis-Hastings algorithm works over evaluation traces and uses exchangeability of random choices. Proposals can be local kernels per primitive.
numbers: Figure 9 shows MH on the sprinkler query. MH for programs that use mem is sketched, not fully proven.
limits: Authors flag chain initialisation under hard constraints as a real challenge. Inference cost is the main limit.
agent_relevance: Generic inference separated from the model is the design lesson: swap the sampler, keep the model.

source: Wingate, Stuhlmuller, Goodman (2011) Lightweight implementations of probabilistic programming languages via transformational compilation
finding: A source-to-source transform gives every random choice an address, so MCMC can run at full speed with small overhead. Bher compiles Church to native Scheme. Stochastic Matlab is built the same way.
numbers: Tested on HMM (sentence length 15, 10,000 samples) and LDA (10 topics, 10 words per doc, 30 word types, 1,000 samples). Bher beat the MIT-Church interpreter on HMM and on small LDA.
limits: MIT-Church scaled better on large LDA because it caches mem results and skips recomputation when inputs are unchanged. Paper says compiled code can run orders of magnitude faster.
agent_relevance: Reuse of unchanged sub-computation decides scaling. Analogue: cache sub-answers across particles.

source: Wingate, Stuhlmuller, Goodman (2011) Lightweight implementations of probabilistic programming languages via transformational compilation
finding: Case study: inverse geological modelling in Stochastic Matlab. A GPU-based deterministic renderer is mixed with stochastic layer parameters to recover layer descriptions from a rock-porosity volume. A dpmem version is compared with a non-dpmem one.
numbers: Gaussian noise at each voxel. Inference-step axis runs to about 400 steps.
limits: Single case study. No error against ground truth in the extracted text.
agent_relevance: Stochastic code can wrap deterministic tools (simulators), like an agent calling a code tool inside a probabilistic step.

source: Frank & Goodman (2012) Predicting pragmatic reasoning in language games
finding: Founding Rational Speech Act (RSA) experiment. A listener infers the referent by Bayes: prior (salience) times likelihood (speaker is informative, utility by surprisal). Three groups bet on a speaker word, on a referent, or on salience.
numbers: Speaker condition N=206, listener condition N=263. Model vs speaker bets r=0.98 (P<0.0001). Model (salience x likelihood) vs listener bets r=0.99; r=0.87 after removing 0 and 100 predictions. Salience vs raw listener bets r=0.19, P=0.40.
quote: speakers choose words proportional to their specificity
limits: Simple two-dimension object sets in one-shot web games. Salience prior was measured, not predicted. Short Brevia paper.
agent_relevance: A tiny probabilistic program that reasons about a speaker fits human pragmatics. For an agent: read intent by asking what a helpful speaker would have said.

source: Goodman & Frank (2016) Pragmatic language interpretation as probabilistic inference
finding: Review of RSA as nested probabilistic programs: a pragmatic listener reasons about a speaker who reasons about a literal listener. Speaker utility is log of literal-listener probability, with cost and epistemic extensions. Used for scalar implicature, hyperbole, irony, metaphor, vague adjectives.
numbers: Betting paradigm: distribute US$100 across options. One study measured quantifier and number-word readings and found RSA predicted them, including the effect of the speaker's limited perceptual access.
limits: Review, so numbers are those of cited studies. Original model uses minimal recursion.
agent_relevance: Treat a user message as evidence about intent under a helpful-speaker model.

source: Goodman & Frank (2016) Pragmatic language interpretation as probabilistic inference
finding: Depth of social recursion is mixed. Several experiments gave chance performance when deeper recursion was needed. One later study found deeper recursion in about 15% of participants. Children: most 5-year-olds accepted 'some horses jumped' when all 3 of 3 did, yet 3-year-olds show implicature in simple signalling games.
numbers: Deeper recursion in about 15% of participants in a complex paradigm. Chance-level in several experiments.
limits: Limited deep-recursion evidence is a boundary condition. Developmental fit is not yet quantitative.
agent_relevance: Keep nested modelling shallow (depth 1-2). Deeper simulation of people is not supported by human data.

source: Lake, Salakhutdinov, Tenenbaum (2015) Human-level concept learning through probabilistic program induction
finding: Bayesian Program Learning (BPL) treats a handwritten character as a generative program of strokes, parts and relations. One-shot classification of Omniglot characters matches people.
numbers: 20-way one-shot errors: people 4.5% (N=40), BPL 3.3%, deep convnet 13.5%, another one-shot deep model 8.0%, Hausdorff distance 34.8%. BPL lesions without compositionality: 11.0% and 14.0% errors.
limits: BPL needs hand-built primitives (strokes). Only handwritten characters. Later deep nets narrowed the gap.
agent_relevance: Compositional program hypotheses beat pattern matching at one-shot generalisation. Supports hypothesis-as-program in a scaffold.

source: Lake, Salakhutdinov, Tenenbaum (2015) Human-level concept learning through probabilistic program induction
finding: Visual Turing tests: judges could barely tell BPL drawings from human ones. Lesioned BPL was easier to detect.
numbers: New-exemplar test: judges at 52% identification level, only 3 of 48 judges reliably above chance. Parsing test N=143 judges: 59% average. Another set N=124. Lesions: no compositionality 68% with 15 of 22 judges above chance; no learning-to-learn 64% with 22 of 45.
limits: 50% is chance. Naive judges, many tests, per-judge significance.
agent_relevance: Ingredients can be tested by lesioning. A scaffold study could ablate operators the same way.

source: Lake, Salakhutdinov, Tenenbaum (2015) Human-level concept learning through probabilistic program induction
finding: Learning to learn from only 5 background alphabets still works for classification but is worse for deep nets.
numbers: BPL 4.3% and 4.0% errors with two different 5-alphabet sets, versus 3.3% with 30 alphabets. Deep nets retrained on 5 alphabets: 24.0% and 22.3% errors.
limits: BPL Turing-test performance degrades with fewer background alphabets.
agent_relevance: Strong priors (a library of strokes) carry data efficiency, not model size.

source: Gerstenberg, Goodman, Lagnado, Tenenbaum (2021) A counterfactual simulation model of causal judgments for physical events
finding: Causal judgments about colliding billiard balls are modelled as noisy counterfactual physics simulation: would the outcome have differed if the candidate cause were removed? Simulation noise is a parameter.
numbers: Experiment 1 (one candidate cause) causal judgments: noise 0.9 gives r=.96, RMSE=13.46. A deterministic model (noise 0) gives r=.86, RMSE=28.15. About N=41 per judgment type.
limits: Uses a physics engine, not a PPL language alone. Two experiments, simple clips, online participants.
agent_relevance: Noise in simulation helps fit. A 'what if this step were removed' check is a cheap causal probe for an agent.

source: Bingham et al. (2018) Pyro: deep universal probabilistic programming
finding: Pyro embeds universal probabilistic programming in Python on PyTorch. It combines stochastic variational inference (SVI) with GPU tensor maths and mini-batches. Stated aims: universal, scalable, minimal, flexible.
numbers: Four principles. SVI is the main engine in the VAE code example.
limits: System paper. The authors say the four goals conflict and trade-offs were made. No benchmark numbers read.
agent_relevance: Modern PPLs are neural-network aware. LLM proposals can slot in as the guide or proposal distribution.

source: Goodman & Stuhlmuller, Design and Implementation of Probabilistic Programming Languages (dippl.org)
finding: WebPPL extends a purely functional subset of JavaScript with random-choice primitives and follows Church. Inference is written with continuations and coroutines. Enumeration costs time proportional to the number of executions (exponential in random choices). Particle filtering often scales better.
numbers: No experimental numbers. Cites Freer & Roy (2012): any computable distribution can be induced by a Church program.
limits: Teaching text. Exact enumeration grows exponentially.
agent_relevance: Enumerate small discrete models exactly. Use particles for large ones.

source: Wong, Grand, Lew, Goodman, Mansinghka, Andreas, Tenenbaum (2023) From word models to world models
finding: Rational meaning construction: an LLM (Codex, few-shot) translates sentences into Church code (the probabilistic language of thought), and Bayesian inference runs on that code. Domains: probabilistic, relational, visual/physical and social reasoning.
numbers: Tug-of-war example: after translation, inference gives about 23.9% chance for one player beating another. Belief flips on new evidence (over 80% falls to 0% when an 'only child' fact contradicts). No benchmark accuracy table.
quote: Church is doing much of the heavy lifting of inference
limits: Illustrative demos, not a measured benchmark. Hand-written domain prompts. Codex picks plausible probabilities from wording ('rarely lazy').
agent_relevance: Closest design to our scaffold idea: the LLM parses to a symbolic model and a separate engine does the inference. Do not let the LLM do the arithmetic.

source: Wong, Grand, Lew, Goodman, Mansinghka, Andreas, Tenenbaum (2023) From word models to world models
finding: Extends the framework with a physics engine, a graphics engine and a planner that translated programs can call. Also discusses how language can build new world models.
numbers: Paper is about 50,000 words and gives no head-to-head accuracy against a plain LLM in the text read.
limits: Position paper with demos. No failure rates stated.
agent_relevance: Tool modules under a probabilistic interface give a path to grounded reasoning.

source: Lew, Zhi-Xuan, Grand, Mansinghka (2023) Sequential Monte Carlo steering of large language models using probabilistic programs
finding: LLaMPPL is a probabilistic programming system for LLM generation. A program defines a Feynman-Kac model over token sequences. SMC with a particle cloud, cloning and culling steers generation under constraints. A trie cache avoids repeated LLM calls across particles.
numbers: Expansion factor K=3 with varying particle counts N. On prompt intersection, mean log Z-hat over 10 runs is higher for the model whose proposal uses logits from both prompts than for one that proposes from a single prompt.
quote: the proposal ... should be as close to the posterior as possible
limits: Quality is shown by log Z-hat (a lower bound on log Z), not by human rating, in the text read. Cost similar to beam search is claimed.
agent_relevance: Proposals should be close to the posterior. Constraint checks as potentials can replace post-hoc filtering in an agent.

source: Lew, Zhi-Xuan, Grand, Mansinghka (2023) Sequential Monte Carlo steering of large language models using probabilistic programs
finding: SMC gives unbiased estimates of the marginal likelihood and of unnormalised posterior integrals. The gap between E[log Z-hat] and log Z upper-bounds the KL between the sampler and the true posterior.
numbers: Unbiasedness holds for the weighted average. Variance depends on the choice of kernel Mt and potential Gt.
limits: Chain-of-thought proposals would break exact proposal density, so weights become approximate.
agent_relevance: Gives a way to score how well a reasoning sampler approximates the true posterior.

source: Ellis (2023) Human-like few-shot learning via Bayesian reasoning over natural language
finding: Hypotheses are stated in natural language and translated to code. An LLM proposes hypotheses, a prior is fine-tuned on human judgments, and Bayes updates on examples. Tested on the number game and on logical concept learning.
numbers: Number game: human data from 8 participants. The fit needs 50-100 proposed hypotheses (about a couple dozen per person). Logical concepts: 112 concepts, 1,596 participants over 25 batches. With 100 proposals per batch the model explains 81% of variance (R2=.81), is within 3% of human accuracy, and beats GPT-4 alone.
quote: GPT-4's judgments are decidedly different from humans
limits: Number game average over only 8 humans. GPT-4 alone gives judgments 'decidedly different from humans'. Tuned prior matters more for logical concepts. A BPL baseline used over 5,000 hypotheses.
agent_relevance: Few LLM-proposed hypotheses plus a Bayes update beat the LLM answering directly. Supports a propose-then-score operator.

source: Ellis (2023) Human-like few-shot learning via Bayesian reasoning over natural language
finding: Switching the hypothesis language from English to Python hurts the fit. Ablating the LLM proposal distribution gives a poor fit because the hypothesis space is too large to guess blindly.
numbers: R2 against sampling budget with 3 seeds, error bars SEM. Variance falls with more samples.
limits: Prior tuning needs human rating data.
agent_relevance: Proposal quality is the bottleneck. A scaffold should spend effort on how hypotheses are generated.

source: Li, Fox, Goodman (2024) Automated statistical model discovery with language models
finding: BoxLM runs Box's Loop with an LM: propose probabilistic programs (pymc), fit by MCMC, criticise via posterior predictive checks and ELPD-LOO, feed statistics back to a critic LM. GPT-4 (gpt4-11-06-preview) proposes.
numbers: Time-series test: held-out MAE on par with Automatic Statistician (greedy GP search), spectral mixture, periodic kernel and N-BEATS baselines. Also compared with open-source expert Stan programs (eight schools, peregrine, dugongs and others).
limits: Dataset leakage handled with simulated analog datasets. Numeric MAE values were not in the extracted text.
agent_relevance: A closed loop of propose, fit, criticise with real numbers fits our critic stage. Probabilistic programs are the model language.

source: Li, Fox, Goodman (2024) Automated statistical model discovery with language models
finding: Metadata in the prompt can hurt. On the peregrine dataset, with metadata BoxLM picked a logistic growth model that misses the early decline. Without metadata it used a quartic polynomial and closed the gap to the expert program.
numbers: Dugongs: with metadata a von Bertalanffy function; without, a polynomial with log inputs. Both fit well.
limits: Two case studies, not a statistical test across many datasets.
agent_relevance: Domain framing can anchor the model to a wrong form. Try a context-stripped pass as a check.

source: Lake, Salakhutdinov, Tenenbaum (2015) Human-level concept learning through probabilistic program induction
finding: People, BPL and other models were compared on five concept-learning tasks that test different forms of generalisation from one or a few examples. The authors say fewer than 25% of judges beat chance on each visual Turing test.
numbers: Five tasks. Fewer than 25% of judges performed significantly above chance on each Turing test. Judges at 51% when new characters were compared with background characters (t(24)=0.497, P>0.05).
limits: Model builds on hand-made stroke primitives and covers perceptual categories only. The authors name planning and explanation as untested.
agent_relevance: A single generative program supports classification, generation and parsing at once. Reuse one world model for several question types.
